title: Cities as Evolutionary Islands: Colonization of Isolated Urban Habitats Promotes Immunogenetic Differentiation in a Common Waterbird
content:
ABSTRACT

Animals that colonize urban landscapes encounter novel selective pressures, including exposure to altered pathogen communities. While these novel selection regimes may promote adaptation, genetic differentiation between urban and non-urban populations may also be driven by demographic history and reflect neutral processes, such as drift. Here, we investigated patterns of immunogenetic differentiation among four pairs of urban and non-urban populations of a common waterbird, the Eurasian coot Fulica atra. To this end, we sampled and genotyped nearly 300 coots at both innate (toll-like receptors, TLRs) and adaptive (major histocompatibility complex, MHC) immune genes involved in pathogen recognition, while microsatellite genotypes were used as a reference for neutral differentiation. We found evidence of immunogenetic differentiation between coots from urban and non-urban landscapes and identified particular immune gene variants and supertypes that differed in frequency between the two landscape types. However, the strongest immunogenetic differentiation was found among individual urban populations, which were also characterized by reduced immunogenetic diversity (allelic richness). Differentiation was higher at immune genes (TLR1LB and MHC class II) than neutral microsatellite loci, suggesting a contribution of selection. Overall, the observed patterns of immunogenetic differentiation likely reflect the combined effects of multiple processes, including independent urban colonization and associated founder effects, drift in spatially isolated urban populations, and selection promoting changes in the immune gene repertoire following each urban colonization event. Our results contribute to the understanding of molecular mechanisms underlying wildlife urbanization and suggest that immune genes, particularly those directly involved in pathogen recognition, may be at the forefront of adaptation to urban life. Our findings highlight the importance of considering immunogenetic variation in the conservation and management of wildlife populations in rapidly expanding urban landscapes.
